p.src: Now Kongming wished to execute Guan Yu. Xuande said, “When the three of us swore brotherhood, we vowed to live and die together. Though Guan Yu has now broken the law, I cannot bear to violate our former oath. I beg you to record his offense for the present and allow him to redeem it through meritorious service.” Only then did Kongming pardon him.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zhou Yu recalled his troops and mustered his commanders, recorded each man’s merit, and reported it to the Marquis of Wu. All the surrendered soldiers they had taken were sent across the river. He lavishly rewarded the three armies, then advanced to seize Nanjun. The vanguard encamped by the river, the entire force being divided into five camps. Zhou Yu occupied the central camp.

p.src: As Zhou Yu was discussing plans for the advance with his officers, a report suddenly came: “Liu Xuande has sent Sun Qian to offer congratulations to the Commander-in-Chief.” Zhou Yu ordered that he be admitted. After completing his salutations, Sun Qian said, “My lord has specially ordered me to offer thanks for the Commander-in-Chief’s great benevolence and to present these modest gifts.” Zhou Yu asked, “Where is Xuande?” Sun Qian replied, “He has now moved his army to Youjiangkou and is encamped there.” Zhou Yu exclaimed in alarm, “Is Kongming also at Youjiang?” Sun Qian said, “Kongming is at Youjiang together with my lord.” Zhou Yu said, “You may return first. I shall come in person to express my thanks.”

p.src: Zhou Yu accepted the gifts and sent Sun Qian back ahead of him. Lu Su asked, “Why did the Commander-in-Chief seem so startled just now?” Zhou Yu said, “Liu Bei has stationed his army at Youjiang; he must intend to seize Nanjun. We have expended so many troops, horses, provisions, and funds, and Nanjun is now within our grasp. Those heartless men mean to take advantage of what we have accomplished—but they must reckon with Zhou Yu while he yet lives!” Lu Su asked, “What plan should we use to drive them away?” Zhou Yu said, “I shall go and speak with him myself. If matters go well, all is well. If not, before he can take Nanjun, I shall finish Liu Bei first!” Lu Su said, “I should like to accompany you.” Thereupon Zhou Yu and Lu Su led three thousand light cavalry straight to Youjiangkou.

p.src: First, Sun Qian returned to Xuande and told him that Zhou Yu would come in person to express his thanks. Xuande then asked Kongming, “What is his purpose in coming?” Kongming laughed and said, “How could he be willing to come and thank us merely for such paltry gifts? He comes solely because of Nanjun.” Xuande asked, “If he comes with troops, how are we to receive him?” Kongming said, “When he arrives, answer him thus and thus.” They then arrayed their warships at Youjiangkou and drew up troops and horses along the shore.

p.src: When word came that Zhou Yu and Lu Su were approaching with troops, Kongming sent Zhao Yun with several horsemen to receive them. Seeing the imposing strength of their forces, Zhou Yu grew deeply uneasy. When they reached the camp gate, Xuande and Kongming welcomed them into the command tent. After the courtesies had been exchanged, a banquet was laid for them. Xuande raised his cup and expressed thanks for the bitter fighting.

p.src: After several rounds of wine, Zhou Yu said, “Governor of Yuzhou, have you moved your troops here because you intend to seize Nanjun?” Xuande replied, “I heard that the Commander-in-Chief meant to take Nanjun, so I came to assist you. If the Commander-in-Chief does not take it, then I certainly shall.” Zhou Yu laughed and said, “We of Eastern Wu have long wished to annex the lands of the Han River. Now Nanjun is already in the palm of my hand—how could I fail to take it?” Xuande said, “Victory and defeat cannot be foretold. When Cao Cao withdrew, he left Cao Ren to guard Nanjun and the surrounding places; he must have devised some extraordinary plan. Moreover, Cao Ren’s valor is irresistible. I fear only that the Commander-in-Chief may be unable to take it.” Zhou Yu said, “If I cannot take it, then you may do as you please and seize it.” Xuande said, “Kongming and Zijing are here as witnesses. Commander-in-Chief, you must not regret your words.”

p.src: Lu Su hesitated and made no reply. Zhou Yu said, “Once a true man has given his word, how could he regret it?” Kongming said, “The Commander-in-Chief’s words are most fair and just. Let Eastern Wu attempt the conquest first. If it fails, what objection could there be to my lord taking it?” Zhou Yu and Lu Su took leave of Xuande and Kongming, mounted their horses, and departed. Xuande asked Kongming, “Sir, you instructed me to answer as I did just now, and though I said the words at the time, the more I turn them over in my mind, the less reasonable they seem. I am now alone and destitute, without so much as a place to set my foot, and I wish to obtain Nanjun merely as a temporary refuge. But if Zhou Yu is allowed to take it first, the city will already belong to Eastern Wu. How then could I settle there?” Kongming laughed heartily and said, “At first I urged you to take Jingzhou, but you would not listen. Have you forgotten that today?” Xuande said, “It formerly belonged to Jingsheng, and so I could not bear to take it. Now it belongs to Cao Cao, so it is only right that I should seize it.” Kongming said, “My lord need not worry. Let Zhou Yu fight to his heart’s content; sooner or later I shall have my lord seated in honor within the city of Nanjun.” Xuande asked, “What plan will accomplish this?” Kongming said, “We need only do thus and thus.” Xuande was delighted. He remained encamped at the river mouth, holding his troops motionless.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zhou Yu and Lu Su returned to camp. Lu Su asked, “Why did the Commander-in-Chief agree to let Xuande take Nanjun?” Zhou Yu said, “I can take Nanjun with a snap of my fingers, so I lose nothing by granting him an empty favor.” He then asked the officers beneath his tent, “Who dares be the first to take Nanjun?” One man answered the call and stepped forward: it was Jiang Qin. Zhou Yu said, “You shall command the vanguard, with Xu Sheng and Ding Feng as your deputies. Take five thousand picked troops and cross the river first. I shall follow with the main force to support you.”

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Ren at Nanjun ordered Cao Hong to defend Yiling, so that the two positions might support each other like the horns of an animal. A man reported, “The troops of Wu have already crossed the Han River.” Cao Ren said, “Our best course is to hold fast and refuse battle.” The valiant cavalry officer Niu Jin stepped forward indignantly and said, “To refuse battle when the enemy has reached the foot of our walls is cowardice. Moreover, our army has newly suffered defeat, and this is precisely the time to revive its fighting spirit. Lend me five hundred picked troops, and I will fight them to the death.”

p.src: Cao Ren consented and ordered Niu Jin to lead five hundred men out to battle. Ding Feng spurred his horse forward to meet him. After they had fought four or five bouts, Ding Feng feigned defeat, and Niu Jin led his troops in pursuit, charging into the enemy formation. Ding Feng directed his troops to surround Niu Jin within the formation in a single encircling ring. Niu Jin charged left and right but could not break free. From the city walls Cao Ren saw Niu Jin trapped at the heart of the encirclement. He donned his armor, mounted his horse, and led several hundred stalwart riders of his retinue out of the city, brandishing his saber with all his might. He hewed his way into the Wu formation. Xu Sheng met him in battle but could not withstand him. Cao Ren fought his way to the center and rescued Niu Jin. Looking back, he saw that several dozen riders were still trapped in the formation and unable to escape, so he wheeled around and charged in once more, rescuing them from the tight encirclement. They then encountered Jiang Qin blocking their path, but Cao Ren and Niu Jin charged with all their strength and scattered his troops. Cao Ren’s younger brother Cao Chun also led troops forward to support them. After a confused melee, the Wu troops were defeated and fled, and Cao Ren returned victorious. Defeated, Jiang Qin returned to Zhou Yu, who angrily wished to execute him, but the other commanders pleaded for his pardon.

p.src: Zhou Yu immediately mustered his troops, intending to fight Cao Ren in person. Gan Ning said, “Commander-in-Chief, you must not act rashly. Cao Ren has now ordered Cao Hong to hold Yiling, forming two mutually supporting positions. Give me three thousand picked troops, and I shall proceed directly to take Yiling; after that, the Commander-in-Chief may seize Nanjun.” Zhou Yu approved his reasoning and first ordered Gan Ning to lead three thousand troops against Yiling. A spy soon reported this to Cao Ren, who consulted with Chen Jiao. Chen Jiao said, “If Yiling is lost, Nanjun too will become indefensible. We should hasten to its relief.” Cao Ren therefore ordered Cao Chun and Niu Jin to lead troops secretly to Cao Hong’s aid. Cao Chun first sent a man to inform Cao Hong and ordered him to leave the city and lure the enemy onward. Gan Ning led his troops to Yiling, and Cao Hong came out to engage him. After more than twenty bouts, Cao Hong fled in defeat. Gan Ning seized Yiling. At dusk, the troops of Cao Chun and Niu Jin arrived. Joining forces from two directions, they surrounded Yiling.

p.src: A scout galloped in to report to Zhou Yu that Gan Ning was trapped within Yiling. Zhou Yu was greatly alarmed. Cheng Pu said, “We must quickly divide our forces and go to his rescue.” Zhou Yu said, “This is a vital strategic position. If we divide our troops to rescue him and Cao Ren leads an attack upon us, what then?” Lü Meng said, “Gan Xingba is one of Jiangdong’s great generals. How can we fail to rescue him?” Zhou Yu said, “I wish to go and rescue him myself; but whom can I leave here to assume my command?” Lü Meng said, “Leave Ling Gongxu to undertake it. I shall lead the vanguard, while you, Commander, bring up the rear; within ten days, we shall surely return in triumph.” Zhou Yu said, “I do not know whether Ling Gongxu will agree to assume my duties for a time.” Ling Tong said, “If the term is ten days, I can undertake it; beyond ten days, the responsibility would be more than I could bear.”

p.src: Zhou Yu was delighted. He left more than ten thousand troops under Ling Tong and that very day led the main army toward Yiling. Lü Meng said to Zhou Yu, “There is a secluded southern path at Yiling that provides a convenient route to Nan Commandery. Send five hundred soldiers to fell trees and block the road. If the enemy is defeated, they are certain to flee by that route. Their horses will be unable to pass, so they will have to abandon them and flee on foot; then we can take their horses.”

p.src: Zhou Yu followed his counsel and dispatched the soldiers. As the main army approached Yiling, Zhou Yu asked, “Who can break through the encirclement and enter the city to rescue Gan Ning?” Zhou Tai volunteered. At once he raised his sword, spurred his horse, and charged straight through Cao’s troops to the foot of the city walls. Seeing Zhou Tai approach, Gan Ning came out of the city to meet him. Zhou Tai told him, “The Commander himself is coming with the army.” Gan Ning ordered his soldiers to make their equipment ready and eat their fill, preparing to attack from within in concert with the rescuers.

p.src: Meanwhile, when Cao Hong, Cao Chun, and Niu Jin heard that Zhou Yu’s army was approaching, they first sent a man to Nan Commandery to inform Cao Ren, while dividing their forces to oppose the enemy. When the Wu army arrived, Cao’s troops went out to meet it. Just as battle was joined, Gan Ning and Zhou Tai charged out along two separate routes. Cao’s troops fell into confusion, and the Wu forces attacked them from every side. As expected, Cao Hong, Cao Chun, and Niu Jin fled along the narrow path; but heaps of felled timber blocked the way, and their horses could not pass, so they all abandoned their mounts and fled on foot. The Wu troops captured more than five hundred horses. Zhou Yu drove his troops onward through the night and reached Nan Commandery, where he encountered Cao Ren’s army coming to relieve Yiling. The two armies met and fought a confused battle. By then night had fallen, and each side withdrew its troops.

p.src: Cao Ren returned to the city and conferred with the others. Cao Hong said, “Now that we have lost Yiling, our position is perilous. Why not open the plan left by the Chancellor and see whether it can deliver us from this danger?” Cao Ren said, “Your words accord exactly with my own thoughts.” He opened the letter and read it, and was overjoyed. He immediately ordered the morning meal to be prepared at the fifth watch; at daybreak, officers and soldiers alike were all to abandon the city; while banners were planted everywhere upon the walls to create a false show of strength, and the army marched out through three gates.

p.src: Now Zhou Yu, having rescued Gan Ning, arrayed his troops outside the walls of Nan Commandery. Seeing Cao’s troops emerge through three gates, Zhou Yu climbed the command platform to observe them. He saw banners planted idly along the battlements, with no one there to guard them; he also saw that every soldier had a bundle strapped about his waist. Zhou Yu privately concluded that Cao Ren must have prepared his escape beforehand. He descended from the platform and gave orders, dividing two forces into left and right wings; if the vanguard won, it was to press forward in pursuit and not withdraw until the gong sounded. He ordered Cheng Pu to command the rear force, while he himself led troops to take the city. When the drums sounded before the opposing formations, Cao Hong rode out and issued a challenge. Zhou Yu came beneath his command banner and sent Han Dang out to engage Cao Hong. After more than thirty bouts, Cao Hong turned and fled in defeat. Cao Ren himself rode out to continue the fight. Zhou Tai spurred his horse forward to meet him. After more than ten bouts, Cao Ren too fled in defeat, and his formation fell into disorder.

p.src: Zhou Yu signaled both wings to charge, and Cao’s army suffered a great defeat. Zhou Yu personally led his forces in pursuit as far as the walls of Nan Commandery. Cao’s troops did not enter the city but fled toward the northwest. Han Dang and Zhou Tai led the vanguard in relentless pursuit. Zhou Yu saw the city gates standing wide open; there was no one upon the walls either, so he ordered his troops to seize the city. Several dozen horsemen entered first. Behind them Zhou Yu spurred his horse onward and rode straight into the barbican. From the gate tower Chen Jiao saw Zhou Yu enter the city in person and secretly cried in admiration, “The Chancellor’s marvelous plan is truly divine!”

p.src: At the crack of a wooden clapper, bows and crossbows loosed from both sides, their volleys falling like a sudden storm. All those who had rushed first into the city tumbled into hidden pits. As Zhou Yu hastily reined in his horse to turn back, a crossbow bolt struck him squarely in the left side, and he toppled from the saddle. Niu Jin charged out of the city to capture Zhou Yu. Xu Sheng and Ding Feng risked their lives to rescue him. Cao’s troops burst out of the city, and the Wu soldiers trampled one another; countless men fell into the trenches and pits. As Cheng Pu hurriedly tried to withdraw the army, Cao Hong and Cao Ren divided their forces and attacked back along two routes. The Wu army was utterly defeated. Fortunately, Ling Tong led a force in a slanting charge from the flank and held off Cao’s troops. Cao Ren led his victorious troops back into the city, while Cheng Pu gathered the defeated army and returned to camp. Ding Feng and Xu Sheng carried Zhou Yu back to his tent. They summoned an army surgeon, who extracted the arrowhead with iron pincers and applied wound medicine to seal the injury. The pain was unbearable, and Zhou Yu could neither eat nor drink. The surgeon said, “The arrowhead was poisoned, so the wound cannot heal quickly. If anger excites him, the wound will break out afresh.” Cheng Pu ordered all three divisions to guard their camps closely and forbade them to venture out lightly. Three days later, Niu Jin led troops out to challenge them, but Cheng Pu held his forces back and made no move. Niu Jin hurled abuse until dusk before returning, and came again the next day to revile them and demand battle. Fearing that Zhou Yu would become angry, Cheng Pu dared not report it to him. On the third day, Niu Jin came right up to the camp gate and shouted abuse, crying again and again that he meant to capture Zhou Yu. Cheng Pu consulted the others, intending to withdraw for the time being, return to the Marquis of Wu, and decide what to do thereafter.

u.src: At the crack of a wooden clapper, bows and crossbows loosed from both sides, their volleys falling like a sudden storm.
All those who had rushed first into the city tumbled into hidden pits.
As Zhou Yu hastily reined in his horse to turn back, a crossbow bolt struck him squarely in the left side, and he toppled from the saddle.
Niu Jin charged out of the city to capture Zhou Yu.
Xu Sheng and Ding Feng risked their lives to rescue him.
Cao’s troops burst out of the city, and the Wu soldiers trampled one another; countless men fell into the trenches and pits.
As Cheng Pu hurriedly tried to withdraw the army, Cao Hong and Cao Ren divided their forces and attacked back along two routes.
The Wu army was utterly defeated.
Fortunately, Ling Tong led a force in a slanting charge from the flank and held off Cao’s troops.
Cao Ren led his victorious troops back into the city, while Cheng Pu gathered the defeated army and returned to camp.

Ding Feng and Xu Sheng carried Zhou Yu back to his tent. They summoned an army surgeon, who extracted the arrowhead with iron pincers and applied wound medicine to seal the injury. The pain was unbearable, and Zhou Yu could neither eat nor drink.
The surgeon said, “The arrowhead was poisoned, so the wound cannot heal quickly.
If anger excites him, the wound will break out afresh.”
Cheng Pu ordered all three divisions to guard their camps closely and forbade them to venture out lightly.
Three days later, Niu Jin led troops out to challenge them, but Cheng Pu held his forces back and made no move.
Niu Jin hurled abuse until dusk before returning, and came again the next day to revile them and demand battle.
Fearing that Zhou Yu would become angry, Cheng Pu dared not report it to him.
On the third day, Niu Jin came right up to the camp gate and shouted abuse, crying again and again that he meant to capture Zhou Yu.
Cheng Pu consulted the others, intending to withdraw for the time being, return to the Marquis of Wu, and decide what to do thereafter.

p.src: Although Zhou Yu suffered from the pain of his wound, he had formed a plan of his own; he already knew that Cao’s troops often came before the camp to hurl abuse, yet none of his generals came to report it. One day, Cao Ren personally led a great army forward, beating drums and raising battle cries as he came to issue a challenge. Cheng Pu held firm and would not come out. Zhou Yu summoned the generals into his tent and asked, “Where are those drums and battle cries coming from?” The generals replied, “The troops are being put through drills.” Zhou Yu angrily said, “Why do you deceive me? I already know that Cao’s troops often come before our camp to revile us. Since Cheng Demou shares command of the army, how dare he sit by and watch?” He then ordered someone to summon Cheng Pu to the tent and questioned him. Cheng Pu said, “I saw that your wound was troubling you, Gongjin, and the surgeon said that you must not be angered. Therefore, though Cao’s troops came to challenge us, I dared not report it.” Zhou Yu said, “If you will not fight, what do you intend to do?” Cheng Pu said, “The generals all wish to withdraw the army and return to Jiangdong for a time. When your arrow wound has healed, we can make further arrangements.”

p.src: When Zhou Yu heard this, he sprang fiercely from his bed and cried, “A true man who receives his lord’s stipend ought to die upon the battlefield; to have his corpse wrapped in horsehide and brought home would be a blessing! How could the affairs of the state be abandoned for the sake of one man—myself?” Having spoken, he immediately donned his armor and mounted his horse. All the officers and soldiers were aghast as he led several hundred horsemen out before the camp. They saw that Cao’s army had already drawn up its formation. Cao Ren sat his horse beneath the command banner, brandishing his whip and reviling them: “Young Zhou Yu is surely doomed to an untimely death! He will never again dare look my army in the face!”

p.src: Before Cao Ren had finished his abuse, Zhou Yu suddenly rode out from among his horsemen and cried, “Cao Ren, you wretch! Do you see Zhou Lang before you?” At the sight of him, all of Cao’s soldiers were astonished and afraid. Cao Ren looked back at his officers and said, “Heap abuse upon him!” The entire army reviled him at the tops of their voices. Zhou Yu flew into a rage and ordered Pan Zhang to ride out and fight. Before the combatants could engage, Zhou Yu suddenly gave a great cry, spurted blood from his mouth, and fell from his horse. Cao’s troops charged forward. Zhou Yu’s generals advanced to hold them off, fought a confused battle, rescued Zhou Yu, and carried him back to his tent.

p.src: Cheng Pu asked, “How is your health, Commander?” Zhou Yu said privately to him, “This is a stratagem of mine.” Cheng Pu asked, “How will the stratagem work?” Zhou Yu replied, “In truth, I am suffering no great pain. I have acted this way so that Cao’s soldiers will hear that I am gravely ill and inevitably underestimate their enemy. We can send trusted soldiers into the city to feign surrender and say that I have died. Cao Ren is certain to raid our camp tonight. I shall lay ambushes on every side to receive him, and then Cao Ren can be captured in a single charge.” Cheng Pu said, “A brilliant stratagem!” At once, wailing arose throughout the camp. The troops were greatly alarmed, and word spread everywhere that the commander’s arrow wound had flared up and killed him; every camp donned mourning.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Ren was conferring with his officers in the city. He said that Zhou Yu’s rage had made his wound burst open, causing him to spit blood and fall from his horse, and that he would surely die before long. While they were discussing this, a sudden report came: “More than ten soldiers from the Wu camp have come to surrender. Among them are two of our own soldiers who were formerly captured by Wu.” Cao Ren hurriedly summoned them and questioned them. The soldiers said, “Today, before the battle lines, Zhou Yu’s wound burst open, and he died as soon as he returned to camp. All his generals have now donned mourning and begun their lamentations. We were humiliated by Cheng Pu, so we have come expressly to surrender and report this news.”

p.src: Cao Ren was delighted and at once proposed raiding the camp that very night, seizing Zhou Yu’s corpse, cutting off his head, and sending it to the capital at Xu. Chen Jiao said, “This plan must be carried out swiftly, without delay.” Cao Ren therefore appointed Niu Jin as vanguard and himself commanded the center, while Cao Hong and Cao Chun brought up the rear. He left only Chen Jiao with a small force to defend the city and mobilized all the remaining troops. At the first watch they left the city and headed straight for Zhou Yu’s main camp. When they reached the camp gate, not a soul was in sight; only unattended banners and spears stood there. Realizing that he had fallen into a trap, Cao Ren hurriedly ordered a retreat. Cannon signals erupted on every side. Han Dang and Jiang Qin charged from the east; Zhou Tai and Pan Zhang from the west; Xu Sheng and Ding Feng from the south; and Chen Wu and Lü Meng from the north. Cao’s army suffered a crushing defeat. All three divisions were scattered and could aid neither van nor rear.

p.src: Cao Ren fought his way out of the encirclement with little more than ten riders. On encountering Cao Hong, he gathered the battered remnants of the army, and together they fled. The fighting lasted until the fifth watch. When they were not far from Nanjun, a drum sounded, and Ling Tong appeared with another force to bar the road and assailed them fiercely. Cao Ren led his men away by a side road, only to meet Gan Ning, who inflicted another fierce attack upon them. Cao Ren dared not return to Nanjun and headed directly for the main road to Xiangyang. The Wu troops pursued them for some distance and then returned.

p.src: Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu recalled their troops and proceeded straight to the walls of Nanjun. There they saw banners everywhere, and a general atop the gate tower called out, “Commander, forgive me! By order of the military strategist, I have already taken the city. I am Zhao Zilong of Changshan.” Zhou Yu flew into a rage and immediately ordered an assault on the city. A storm of arrows shot down from the walls. Zhou Yu ordered a temporary withdrawal to deliberate. He sent Gan Ning with several thousand troops to seize Jingzhou directly, and Ling Tong with several thousand troops to seize Xiangyang directly. Afterward, it would not be too late to return and take Nanjun.

p.src: As these assignments were being made, a scout suddenly galloped up and reported: “After taking Nanjun, Zhuge Liang used the military tally to issue a false, urgent summons by night, ordering Jingzhou’s garrison to come to the rescue; meanwhile, he had Zhang Fei seize Jingzhou by surprise.” Another scout galloped up and reported: “At Xiangyang, Xiahou Dun was approached by a messenger sent by Zhuge Liang bearing the military tally. The messenger falsely claimed that Cao Ren required aid and lured Xiahou Dun into leading his troops out; meanwhile, Guan Yu was sent to seize Xiangyang by surprise. Both cities were taken without the least effort and now belong to Liu Xuande.” Zhou Yu said, “How did Zhuge Liang obtain the military tally?” Cheng Pu replied, “Once he captured Chen Jiao, all the military tallies naturally fell into his hands.” Zhou Yu gave a great cry, and his wound burst open.
